Family Health

Using condoms correctly and responding to a break or slip

Updated: October 5, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Condoms can help prevent pregnancy and reduce the risk of sexually transmitted infections, or STIs. Their protection depends on using an appropriate product correctly throughout sex. A damaged packet, poor fit, unsuitable lubricant or putting a condom on late can reduce that protection. Knowing the steps in advance (and knowing where to get help after a problem) makes prevention easier to share.

What condoms can and cannot protect against

An external condom covers an erect penis and collects semen after ejaculation. An internal condom is a pouch worn inside the body, with its outer ring remaining outside during vaginal use. Both provide a physical barrier, although their instructions and evidence are not identical.

External condoms are used for vaginal, anal and oral sex. They reduce contact with fluids and covered skin, but they cannot protect every area of skin. Some infections can pass through contact with areas that a condom does not cover.

Condoms reduce risk; they do not promise that pregnancy or an STI is impossible. Their success also depends on using a new one for each act and keeping it in place from beginning to end. A hormonal contraceptive or an IUD may add pregnancy protection, but does not replace a barrier for STI prevention.

Check the packet, expiry date and condition

Before use, read the expiry date on the individual wrapper and the box when available. Use an in-date product with an intact wrapper. A recognised quality or regulatory mark appropriate to your country can help you choose a properly tested product.

Open the wrapper carefully with your fingers. Teeth, scissors, sharp nails and jewellery can damage the condom. If the wrapper is torn, punctured or looks badly worn, choose another one rather than trying to decide how much damage is acceptable.

After opening, do not use a condom that is brittle, sticky, torn or unexpectedly discoloured, or has an unusual smell or texture for that product. Lubrication and flavouring vary, so the aim is to notice damage or an unexpected change, not to assume every lubricated product is defective.

Fading or rubbing on a wrapper does not prove the condom inside has failed, but it can suggest poor storage or wear. When in doubt, replace it. Looking normal is also not a reason to use an expired product.

Choose a fit and material that suit you

A condom should fit securely without being painfully tight and should unroll as intended. One that is too loose may slip; an unsuitable tight fit can make use uncomfortable or contribute to problems. If the same issue keeps happening, try another size or shape or ask a sexual-health service for advice.

Latex is common, but polyurethane or polyisoprene alternatives may be suitable for people with a latex allergy. Check the material on the packet and whether the product is intended for the type of sex you are planning.

Natural-membrane products, sometimes sold as lambskin condoms, should not be relied on for HIV or other STI prevention. They are different from synthetic latex-free condoms. “Latex-free” alone is not enough information to choose a product for infection protection.

If a product causes itching, soreness or another reaction, stop using it and seek advice about the cause and alternatives. Lubricant, fragrance or spermicide can also irritate; not every reaction is a latex allergy.

How to put on an external condom

1. Have the condom ready before sexual contact. With the penis fully erect, open the packet carefully and check the condom. If there is a foreskin, gently retract it as comfortable before placement. Do not force a painful or tight foreskin.

2. Check that the rolled rim faces outward so the condom can roll down. Pinch the reservoir tip to expel trapped air and leave room to collect semen. Place it on the head of the penis before genital, oral or anal contact.

3. Keeping the tip pinched, roll the condom down to the base. If it will not unroll because it is the wrong way round, discard it and use a new one. Do not simply flip it over: fluid on the first side could then contact your partner.

4. Use a compatible lubricant when needed to reduce friction. Check during sex that the condom remains in place. Stop if it rolls up, slips, breaks or feels damaged. Add suitable lubricant if friction increases rather than continuing with a dry or uncomfortable barrier.

Removing an external condom without spilling

After ejaculation or when sex is finished, hold the condom firmly at the base while withdrawing. Withdraw while the penis is still erect so that a loosening fit does not allow the condom to slide off.

Move away from your partner’s genitals before removing it. Keep semen inside, wrap the condom in tissue if helpful and place it in a rubbish bin. You may close or tie the opening to reduce spilling. Never reuse it or put it in the toilet.

Use a new condom for another act of sex, for a different partner and when changing between anal and vaginal contact. A condom used for practice is also a used condom and should be discarded.

How to use an internal condom for vaginal sex

1. Check the instructions and wrapper, then open it gently. Find a comfortable position, such as lying down or standing with one foot supported. Identify the closed end with the inner ring and the open end with the outer ring.

2. Squeeze the inner ring between your fingers and guide the closed end into the vagina. Use a finger inside the pouch to push the inner ring comfortably upward. It sits high in the vagina near the cervix; it is not pushed through the cervix.

3. Make sure the pouch is not twisted. The outer ring must stay outside the vaginal opening. Guide the penis into the pouch, checking that it has not passed between the condom and the vaginal wall.

4. Stop if the outer ring is pushed inside, the penis goes outside the pouch or the condom slips or tears. Do not keep having sex while trying to pull it back into place. Replace it before continuing and consider whether pregnancy or STI exposure advice is needed.

5. To remove it, gently twist the outer ring to keep fluid inside and carefully pull the pouch out. Put it in the bin after one use. Do not combine an internal condom with an external condom; friction between them can cause damage.

Internal condoms and anal use need specific guidance

Internal condoms are sometimes used for anal sex, but the evidence for effectiveness in that setting is more limited than for established vaginal use. Product authorisation and instructions can also vary.

Do not assume the vaginal insertion steps transfer unchanged to every product or body site. Ask a sexual-health clinician or follow an appropriate manufacturer’s guide for the intended use. An external condom with compatible lubricant is another barrier option for anal sex.

Whichever method you choose, use one barrier at a time, check that it is positioned correctly and stop if it moves out of place. No barrier should be forced into a painful position.

Dental dams and condoms for oral sex

A dental dam is a thin sheet, commonly latex or polyurethane, placed between the mouth and the vulva or anus during oral sex. It is not a condom to insert for vaginal or anal intercourse, and it is not a contraceptive method for penetrative sex.

Check the expiry date and condition, open the packet without damaging the sheet and place it flat over the area before oral contact. Hold it in place throughout. Do not stretch it tightly, turn it over during use or move it from one body site to another.

Use a lubricant that the product allows if needed, and replace the dam if it tears or slips so that contact is no longer covered. Afterward, fold it carefully and put it in the bin. Use a new sheet next time.

For oral contact with a penis, use an external condom before contact begins and follow the same careful placement and removal principles. If choosing a flavoured product, check its intended use and any allergy or irritation concerns. A flavour or texture is not an extra safety guarantee.

Match lubricant to the condom material

Lubricant can reduce friction and improve comfort, particularly when natural lubrication is limited. It does not make a damaged condom safe or remove the need to check fit and placement.

Water-based or silicone-based lubricant is generally compatible with condoms. With latex or polyisoprene condoms, avoid oil-based products such as petroleum jelly, baby oil, body lotion, massage oil or cooking oil: they can weaken the material.

Polyurethane has different compatibility, and some polyurethane products permit oil-based lubricant. Check the instructions for the exact condom or dam rather than treating all latex-free products alike. If uncertain, choose a condom-compatible water-based or silicone-based product.

Creams or medicines applied to the genitals can also affect compatibility. Read their instructions or ask a pharmacist. If a toy is involved, check the toy’s lubricant instructions too; a lubricant can be compatible with the condom but unsuitable for the toy material.

Should you add spermicide?

Spermicide is not required for routine condom use and does not add protection against STIs. Products containing nonoxynol-9 can irritate genital or rectal tissue; frequent use has been associated with increased vulnerability to HIV. It should not be added as an infection-prevention measure.

A spermicide-coated condom should not be assumed to provide better protection than a condom without spermicide. If avoiding pregnancy is especially important, discuss adding a separate effective contraceptive method rather than assuming spermicide makes a condom failure-proof.

If you choose a vaginal spermicide as part of a contraception plan, follow that product’s directions for timing, placement and repeat use. There is no universal thirty-to-sixty-minute rule for every formulation. Do not spread a vaginal product on an oral barrier or use it rectally unless it is specifically intended and recommended for that use.

What to do after use: and why a water test is not reassurance

Dispose of used condoms and dams in a bin. Do not wash and reuse them or flush them down the toilet. Their material and fit are designed for a single use, and flushing can block plumbing.

Filling a used condom with water is not a reliable way to prove that no pregnancy or STI exposure occurred. A condom may have slipped, been put on late or allowed contact outside the covered area even if you see no leaking hole afterward.

If you noticed a break, slippage or spill, or are uncertain whether the condom was used throughout, act on that history. Do not delay advice while trying home tests of the used condom.

If a condom breaks or slips during sex

Stop as soon as you notice the problem. Remove the damaged or displaced condom and use a new one if you decide to continue. Replace a damaged dental dam as well. A fresh barrier helps with later contact but cannot undo exposure that has already happened.

Consider the kind of contact and whether semen could have reached the vagina. If pregnancy is possible, contact a pharmacist, sexual-health clinic or clinician promptly about emergency contraception. They can also assess the need for STI advice based on the exposure.

If a condom is stuck and cannot be removed easily, seek medical help rather than using sharp tools. If you have pain, bleeding or injury, describe those symptoms when asking for care. There is no need to feel embarrassed about requesting help.

Emergency contraception is time-sensitive

Emergency pills and a copper IUD are possible options after sex that could result in pregnancy. Seek advice as soon as possible. Some options can be used within five days, but the best choice depends on timing, medicines, other contraception and individual circumstances.

Ulipristal can be used up to 120 hours after sex. Levonorgestrel works best when taken sooner; some local instructions specify 72 hours, and effectiveness declines with delay. A clinician can assess whether a copper IUD is suitable, including situations where its timing is based on likely ovulation.

Do not assume every option is “95% effective” or that waiting until day five makes no difference. Ask what to do about regular hormonal contraception afterward, because restart advice differs after ulipristal and levonorgestrel. Emergency pills do not protect sex that happens later.

Follow the pregnancy-testing advice given with treatment. If testing too early, a negative result may miss a pregnancy. Ask the pharmacist or clinician when to test and when to repeat it, especially if the next period is delayed or unusual.

STI testing and urgent HIV prevention

Emergency contraception does not prevent STIs. A sexual-health service can advise which tests are relevant, whether testing should be done now and when it should be repeated. An immediate negative result cannot rule out every recent infection because tests have different window periods.

If there may have been a significant HIV exposure, ask urgently about post-exposure prophylaxis, or PEP. It must be started within 72 hours, and earlier is better. Do not wait for symptoms or routine test results before seeking that assessment.

Not every condom problem requires PEP, but the decision should be made promptly by a clinician. For ongoing risk, a service can also discuss testing, vaccination where appropriate and other prevention options.

Store supplies well and plan together

Keep condoms and dams somewhere cool and dry, away from direct sunlight, heat and repeated rubbing. A wallet carried for long periods, a hot car or a damp bathroom can be a poor storage place. A bag is not automatically unsafe, but the product needs protection from heat, sharp objects and friction.

Have a spare available and practise opening and using a condom before you need it if that would help you feel confident. Do not reuse the practice condom. Check older supplies periodically so that an expired packet is not your only option.

Some sexual-health clinics and community services provide condoms free or at low cost; availability depends on where you live. Ask about sizes, latex-free options and suitable lubricant if access or cost is a concern.

Talk with your partner about contraception, STI prevention, comfort and what you would do if a barrier failed. Different sizes, materials, textures or flavours can be considered together, with intended use and comfort guiding the choice. Protection is a shared practical responsibility.

Using a condom alongside a suitable hormonal method or IUD can address both infection risk and pregnancy prevention. It does not mean wearing two condoms. Planning ahead can reduce uncertainty without promising that any method removes every risk.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

CDC and NHS guidance emphasizes correct use from start to finish, a new barrier for each act, suitable lubricant and stopping when a condom slips or breaks. Condoms reduce risk but do not cover every possible route of STI transmission.

CDC guidance distinguishes emergency contraception from STI prevention. It also identifies a short window for HIV PEP after a relevant exposure. Spermicide and a home water test do not replace those assessments.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama’s guide to prepare supplies, check product instructions and plan where to seek help after a problem. It offers general education, not a personalised assessment of pregnancy or infection risk. A pharmacist or sexual-health clinician can help choose the next step.

When to seek help

Seek prompt advice after a condom break or slip if pregnancy or STI exposure is possible. HIV PEP assessment is urgent because treatment must begin within 72 hours. Get medical help for a retained condom you cannot remove, significant pain, bleeding or injury.

Evidence notes updated: October 5, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Check expiry, wrapper, fit and material before use.
  • Use one new condom throughout each act; do not double up.
  • Stop if an internal condom is displaced or the penis passes outside its pouch.
  • Oil can damage latex and polyisoprene; follow material-specific lubricant instructions.
  • Spermicide does not add STI protection.
  • After a break or slip, seek time-sensitive pregnancy and STI advice.

Frequently asked questions

Can I wear two condoms for extra protection?

No. Two external condoms, or an external and internal condom together, can rub and tear. Use one correctly fitted condom and consider a separate contraceptive method if desired.

Can I turn a condom over if I started putting it on backward?

Use a new one. Fluid on the first side could contact your partner if you flip it over.

Is oil safe with every latex-free condom?

No. Polyisoprene can be damaged by oil. Some polyurethane products allow it, but check the exact product’s instructions.

What if the internal condom’s outer ring goes inside?

Stop intercourse. Replace the condom before continuing and seek advice if there may have been pregnancy or STI exposure.

Does spermicide make a condom safer against infections?

No. Nonoxynol-9 can irritate tissue and is not recommended for STI or HIV prevention.

Does filling a used condom with water prove it worked?

No. It cannot rule out slippage, late application, spills or uncovered contact. Base follow-up on what happened during sex.

How quickly should I ask about emergency contraception?

As soon as possible. Options have different time windows, and some can be used within five days. A pharmacist or clinician can advise what is suitable.

Can I wait for an HIV test before asking about PEP?

Do not delay assessment. If an exposure may warrant PEP, it must be started within 72 hours and is best started earlier. The clinician will arrange appropriate testing.

Do natural-membrane condoms prevent STIs?

They should not be relied on for HIV or other STI prevention. Choose an appropriate latex or synthetic product if infection protection is needed.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
